title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of making AI education more accessible and relevant for K–12 teachers and learners by integrating AI concepts into core non-computing subjects. The authors argue that many existing AI curricula are standalone or computer-science-centered, which makes them difficult for teachers of English, social studies, science, and other subjects to adopt. They investigate what K–12 teachers need in order to design and potentially implement integrated AI curricula.

The study used a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K–12 educators from a range of subjects and grade levels. The workshop included presentations to establish shared AI knowledge, tool demonstrations, a card-sorting activity, a pre-work assignment in which teachers connected one AI tool to their own curriculum, and co-design sessions where teachers and researchers worked in small groups to draft integrated lesson plans. The researchers analyzed workshop audio, questionnaires, and participant artifacts using open coding.

The resulting curricula embedded AI into social studies, ESL, literacy for students with learning disabilities, and an exemplar physics curriculum. Across the workshops, teachers emphasized four design needs: evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration. The paper concludes that integrated AI curriculum should leverage data already produced in classroom activities, support student reflection, and include explicit scaffolding for ethics. It also notes that teacher-researcher co-design, even in a remote format, can surface practical pathways for making AI education more accessible beyond computing classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / AI learning tool category; in this paper, the workshop explored several AI learning tools rather than a single named GenAI product.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers co-designed integrated K-12 lesson plans around AI learning tools and discussed how AI concepts could be embedded into core subjects. The paper references tools such as Teachable Machine, Machine Learning for Kids, Google Quick, Draw!, MIT App Inventor AI, Arbitrary Style Transfer, and related AI learning tools as examples used in the workshop.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative co-design study about teacher needs and curriculum design, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool’s learning effects. The methodology is clear, but it does not test a specific product or report causal outcome data.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has meaningful design implications for K-12 AI curriculum implementation, but it does not measure student achievement or compare tool impacts. As a result, impact is important but indirect and not quantifiable from the study.
